name: AI Travel Companions
objectives: Using a free AI assistant, ask for a day-by-day trip plan that says where, when, who is going, your interests and your pace, with rest time and no more activities than you can comfortably do
Given an AI trip plan, check important facts such as hours, prices and ID rules on official websites, checking at least three facts before you rely on them
Given your trip and health needs, ask for a grouped packing list that includes your medicines and ID, with medicines and ID in your carry-on bag
Using a maps app on your phone, get walking, driving or transit directions and follow the spoken turns, with your hotel saved as a favorite
When you need another language, use a translation app to read a sign or have a simple conversation, with important needs, such as allergies, written ahead and checked with staff
Before and during a trip, share your plans with family and spot travel scams, booking only through official sites or trusted agents

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Planning a relaxed itinerary with AI
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Ask an AI assistant for a day-by-day trip plan that fits your pace.
This lesson builds toward: Using a free AI assistant, you will ask for a day-by-day trip plan that says where, when, who is going, your interests and your pace, with rest time and no more activities than you can comfortably do.
An itinerary is a day-by-day plan for a trip. An AI assistant can draft one in seconds, and change it as often as you like.
Tell it where, when, how long, who is going, and what you need: "Plan a relaxed three-day trip to Savannah, Georgia in April for two people in their 70s. We like history and gardens, walk slowly, and want a rest every afternoon. No more than two activities a day."
Ask for changes until it fits: "Add a place to sit and have lunch near each morning activity." "Which places have elevators or are easy for someone with a cane?"
Step by step:
- Say where, when and how long.
- Say who is going and what you enjoy.
- Say your pace and any needs, such as rest or easy walking.
- Ask for changes until it fits you.
Words to know:
- Itinerary: a day-by-day plan for a trip.
- Accessible: easy to reach and use for people with limited mobility, hearing or sight.
Try it now: Pick a trip you would like to take. Ask an AI assistant for a relaxed three-day itinerary with your pace and needs, then ask for one change.
You can now ask AI for a trip plan that fits your pace and needs.

options: A day-by-day plan for a trip
check.why: An itinerary is a day-by-day trip plan that AI can draft and change.

check.q: The AI plan has four activities a day and you tire easily. What do you ask?
options: "No more than two activities a day, with a rest each afternoon."
check.why: Ask for changes until the plan fits your pace and needs.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Checking travel facts on official sites
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Check the important facts in an AI trip plan before you rely on them.
This lesson builds toward: Given an AI trip plan, you will check important facts such as hours, prices and ID rules on official websites, checking at least three facts before you rely on them.
AI trip plans can include mistakes: a museum that closed, old opening hours, wrong prices or rules that changed. Always check the facts that could spoil your trip.
Check opening hours and prices on the place's own website. Check flights and train times with the airline or rail company. For ID: since May 7, 2025, travelers flying within the United States need a REAL ID-compliant license or ID card, or another accepted ID such as a passport. TSA's website, tsa.gov, lists all accepted IDs.
Ask the assistant: "What in this plan should I double-check?" It can point out the facts that matter, but you check them on the official sites.
Step by step:
- Ask AI which facts to double-check.
- Check hours and prices on each place's own website.
- Check flight or train times with the company.
- Check ID rules on tsa.gov before flying.
Words to know:
- REAL ID: a driver's license or state ID that meets federal rules; it usually has a star in the corner.
- TSA: the Transportation Security Administration, which screens travelers at US airports.
Official sources:
- TSA: REAL ID
Try it now: Ask the assistant which facts in your itinerary to double-check. Then check the opening hours of one place on its own website, and check whether your ID is REAL ID-compliant (look for the star) or what else tsa.gov accepts.
You can now check the key facts in an AI trip plan on official websites.

check.q: Where do you check a museum's opening hours?
check.why: AI can give old hours; the place's own website has the current ones.

check.q: You plan to fly within the US and are not sure your ID is accepted. What do you do?
options: Ask the AI and trust it
Check the list of accepted IDs on tsa.gov
check.why: TSA's website, tsa.gov, lists all accepted IDs for flying.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Making a smart packing list
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 4 minutes
Goal: Ask AI for a packing list that fits your trip and your health needs.
This lesson builds toward: Given your trip and health needs, you will ask for a grouped packing list that includes your medicines and ID, with medicines and ID in your carry-on bag.
A packing list stops the classic travel worry: "Did I forget something?" Ask the assistant for one based on your trip, the season and the activities.
For example: "Make a packing list for three days in Savannah in April. I take daily medicines and use reading glasses and a hearing aid. Group it by: documents, medicines and health, clothes, and electronics."
Keep medicines in your carry-on bag in their original containers, with a little extra in case of delays, and bring a list of your medicines and doctor's phone number. Your pharmacist can advise on travel with medicines.
Step by step:
- Tell AI the place, season, length and activities.
- Mention health needs, such as medicines or hearing aids.
- Ask it to group the list.
- Keep medicines and ID in your carry-on bag.
Words to know:
- Carry-on bag: the bag you keep with you on a plane, bus or train.
Try it now: Ask an AI assistant for a grouped packing list for your trip, including your health needs. Add anything it forgot, and save or print the list.
You can now make a packing list with AI that includes your health needs.

check.q: Why ask AI to group a packing list?
options: So it is easy to check by section, such as documents and medicines
So the AI remembers your trip
check.why: Grouping by documents, medicines, clothes and electronics makes the list easy to check.

check.q: You take daily medicines. How do you pack them?
options: In your carry-on, in original containers, with a little extra
check.why: Keep medicines in your carry-on in original containers, with extra in case of delays.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Using maps and directions on your phone
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Get walking or driving directions with a maps app.
This lesson builds toward: Using a maps app on your phone, you will get walking, driving or transit directions and follow the spoken turns, with your hotel saved as a favorite.
Maps apps such as Google Maps and Apple Maps show where you are and how to get where you are going, by car, on foot or by public transit.
Open the maps app and type the place in the search box, or say it to your voice assistant: "Hey Siri, walking directions to Forsyth Park." Tap Directions, choose walking, driving or transit, then tap Start. The app speaks each turn.
Before a trip, save your hotel as a favorite place, so getting back is just one tap. Directions use your phone's battery, so bring a charger or small battery pack.
Step by step:
- Open your maps app.
- Type or say where you want to go.
- Tap Directions and choose walking, driving or transit.
- Tap Start and follow the spoken turns.
- Save your hotel as a favorite.
Words to know:
- GPS: a system that lets your phone know where you are on a map.
- Transit: public transportation such as buses and trains.
Try it now: Use your maps app to get walking directions from your home to a nearby store or park. Tap Start and listen to the first instruction.
You can now get and follow directions with a maps app.

check.q: What does Transit mean in a maps app?
check.why: Transit means public transport, such as buses and trains.

check.q: You are out walking and want an easy way back to your hotel. What should you have done before the trip?
options: Saved the hotel as a favorite place in the maps app
Written the hotel's name on your hand
check.why: Saving the hotel as a favorite makes getting back one tap.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Talking and reading in another language
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Use a translation app to read a sign or have a simple conversation.
This lesson builds toward: When you need another language, you will use a translation app to read a sign or have a simple conversation, with important needs, such as allergies, written ahead and checked with staff.
Traveling abroad, or meeting a new in-law who speaks another language? Translation apps such as Google Translate and the iPhone's Translate app can help.
Type or speak a sentence and it shows and speaks the translation. Conversation mode lets two people take turns speaking. Camera mode lets you point your phone at a sign or menu and see it in your language.
Translations are good but not perfect. For important matters, such as medical needs or allergies, carry a card in the local language written ahead of time, and check it with a hotel or pharmacy staff member. Many apps let you download a language before you go, so it works without internet.
Step by step:
- Open a translation app and choose the two languages.
- Type or speak your sentence.
- Use conversation mode to take turns.
- Use camera mode for signs and menus.
- Download the language before you travel.
Words to know:
- Translate: to change words from one language into another.
- Offline: working without an internet connection.
Try it now: Open a translation app. Translate "Where is the restroom, please?" into a language you might need, and listen to it spoken aloud.
You can now use a translation app to speak, read signs and menus, and prepare for important needs.

check.q: What does camera mode in a translation app do?
options: Shows a sign or menu in your language when you point the phone at it
check.why: Camera mode translates what the phone camera sees, such as signs and menus.

check.q: You will be somewhere with no internet. What do you do before you go?
options: Download the language in the app
check.why: Many apps let you download a language so they work offline.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Staying safe and connected while traveling
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Share your plans and location with family and avoid travel scams.
This lesson builds toward: Before and during a trip, you will share your plans with family and spot travel scams, booking only through official sites or trusted agents.
Let family know where you are. Share your itinerary with a family member, and consider sharing your location from your phone for the trip (on iPhone, the Find My app; on Android, Google Maps location sharing). You can stop sharing anytime.
Watch out for travel scams: fake booking websites, calls saying you "won" a trip, and messages about problems with your flight that ask you to call a strange number or pay. Book through the airline's, hotel's or train company's own website or a trusted agent, and check any message by calling the number on their official website.
Keep a copy of your ID and medicine list in a safe place apart from the originals, and avoid entering bank details on public Wi-Fi in hotels or airports.
Step by step:
- Share your itinerary with a family member.
- Turn on location sharing for the trip if you wish.
- Book only through official sites or trusted agents.
- Check travel messages on the company's official number.
- Avoid banking on public Wi-Fi.
Words to know:
- Location sharing: letting chosen people see where your phone is on a map.
- Public Wi-Fi: free wireless internet in places like hotels and airports, which others can share.
Try it now: Final task: finish your three-day trip plan with a comfortable pace and rest time, your packing list with medicines and ID, and three facts you checked on official websites. Share the plan with a family member.
You can now plan a trip with AI, check it, pack for it, find your way, and stay safe and connected.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Comfortable plan No day-by-day plan, or too many activities with no rest. A three-day plan, day by day, at a comfortable pace with rest time. The plan also notes places to sit or easy access where needed. Packing list No list, or medicines or ID are missing. A grouped packing list that includes medicines and ID. Notes that medicines and ID go in the carry-on, with a medicine list and doctor's number. Facts checked Fewer than three facts checked, or checked only with the AI. Three facts checked on official websites, such as tsa.gov and a place's own site. Can say which site each fact came from and fixed anything that was wrong. Shared with family The plan was not shared. The plan was shared with a family member. Also agreed on location sharing for the trip or a check-in time. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

options: Shows everyone online where you are
Lets family you choose see where your phone is
check.why: Location sharing shows your phone's location to the people you choose, and you can stop anytime.

check.q: A website offers your hotel at half price if you pay by wire transfer today. What do you do?
options: Ask the website if it is real
Book through the hotel's own website or a trusted agent
check.why: Fake booking sites are common; book only through official sites or trusted agents.
